sections.h2: Where is Medford, Massachusetts, and how is it divided?
sections.html:
Medford is a city in Middlesex County, north of Boston, and the Mystic River runs from west to southeast through the middle of it. It covers 8.66 square miles and had 59,659 residents at the 2020 census.

Part of the 2,060 acre Middlesex Fells Reservation lies in the north, shared with Winchester, Stoneham, Melrose and Malden. Tufts University has its campus along the Medford and Somerville line.

People in Medford usually name their neighborhood first, and each has its own feel.

  • West Medford, described as the most affluent area, with a historic African American neighborhood dating to the Civil War.
  • South Medford, traditionally Italian.
  • Wellington, also called East Medford.
  • Fulton Heights, or The Heights, in North Medford.
  • Brooks Estates, Glenwood, Lawrence Estates and Medford Hillside, where Tufts is mostly situated.

Irish Americans live throughout the city. If you list or sell to a buyer, the neighborhood name tells them more about a house than the city name does, so use it.

sections.h2: What is the history of Medford?
sections.html:
English colonists settled Medford in 1630 as part of Charlestown, and it became a city in 1892.

The first toll bridge across the Mystic River went up in 1637 where the Cradock Bridge stands today, and it carried Main Street into Medford Square. For roughly 150 years it was the only bridge over the Mystic, which made Medford a crossing point into Boston from the north.

Medford was a center of industry. It made tiles, crackers, bricks, rum and clipper ships, such as the White Swallow and the Kingfisher. Tufts was chartered in 1852. The Boston and Maine Railroad reached Medford Center in 1847, and farmland was divided into lots for houses starting in the 1840s and 1850s.

Historic sites include the Peter Tufts House at 350 Riverside Avenue, thought to be the oldest all-brick building in New England, and the Royall House and Slave Quarters, a National Historic Landmark. Houses in the old Ship Street Historic District around Riverside Avenue are some of the oldest, and an old house can mean old systems.

sections.h2: How do you get around Medford?
sections.html:
Medford has both Orange Line and Green Line subway service, plus a commuter rail stop and many bus routes.

ServiceWhere in Medford
Orange LineWellington station, opened in 1975
Green LineMedford/Tufts and Ball Square, opened in 2022 as part of the GLX project
Commuter Rail, Lowell LineWest Medford
MBTA busesRoutes 80, 94, 95, 96, 99, 100, 101, 108 and 134, plus express route 354

Interstate 93 runs north and south through the city, and state routes 16, 28, 38 and 60 cross it. Houses close to the new Green Line stops sit in a part of the city where transit changed recently, which can matter to buyers of all kinds.

Medford Public Schools run two high schools, Medford High School and Medford Vocational Technical High School.

  • Middle schools: John J. McGlynn and Madeline Dugger Andrews.
  • Elementary schools: Missituk, Brooks, John J. McGlynn and Milton Fuller Roberts.
  • Private schools: St. Joseph's (K to 8) and St. Raphael's (pre-K to 8).
  • College: Tufts University.

The Medford and Malden high school Thanksgiving game dates from 1889. Ask the district office which school your street feeds, since this page cannot confirm attendance zones.

sections.h2: How do Tufts and the local economy affect Medford sellers?
sections.html:
Tufts University is the best known institution in Medford, and the Tufts campus straddles the Medford and Somerville line, mostly on Medford Hillside. The university employs many local residents and runs community service projects with the city.

  • The median age in Medford is 35.6, and 14.1 percent of residents are under 18.
  • About 28.5 percent of households are one person.
  • Medford is governed by a mayor and a city council with a separate school committee.
  • The Meadow Glen Mall closed on February 1, 2016, and its site was being prepared for a retail plaza.

Owners of rental houses sometimes decide to sell after repeated turnover, damage or a change in family plans, and a cash buyer can take on a house with tenants or one left vacant. Tell the buyer which applies.

sections.h2: What should a Medford seller handle before closing?
sections.html:
A Massachusetts seller needs a certificate of compliance for smoke and carbon monoxide alarms from the local fire department, according to the Department of Fire Services.

The state tells owners to learn the year the house was built and the date of its last building permit, list each alarm and its manufacture date, and replace alarms that are expired or undated. Battery smoke alarms older than 10 years must be replaced with sealed 10 year photoelectric alarms that have a hush feature. After installing them, test them, then call the Medford fire department, which charges a fee for the inspection and certificate.

The deed excise under Chapter 64D, Section 1 is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of price or fraction of it, outside Barnstable County. Deeds are recorded at a county registry. Medford's county, Middlesex, has a South registry in Cambridge and a North registry in Lowell. Ask Medford's city offices about permits, open violations and any tax bills before you close.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale of a Medford house work?
sections.html:
With a cash sale the buyer does not wait on a mortgage lender, so the closing date follows your needs.

  1. You share the address, condition, tenants if any and your timing.
  2. The buyer reviews the house and sends a written offer.
  3. You accept, and a Massachusetts attorney handles title and the purchase and sale agreement.
  4. The alarm certificate and any payoffs get arranged.
  5. The deed is recorded and you receive the proceeds.

An offer should reflect the house itself, so ask any buyer how they arrive at their number. Compare the net result with listing, including repairs, showings and months of carrying costs.

faqs.q: How many people live in Medford, MA?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 59,659 residents in Medford, living in 24,413 households. The Census Bureau ranked it among the nation's fastest growing populations between 2021 and 2022.

faqs.q: Is Medford close to the T?
faqs.a: Yes. Wellington is on the Orange Line, and Medford/Tufts and Ball Square are on the Green Line, which opened in 2022. West Medford has Lowell Line commuter rail.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Medford?
faqs.a: Yes. The Department of Fire Services says a certificate of compliance from the local fire department is required when you sell or transfer a home. Call the Medford fire department for the fee and scheduling.

faqs.q: What is the deed excise tax when I sell in Medford?
faqs.a: It is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of the sale price or fraction of it. A $700,000 sale produces $2,800. Your contract and attorney will confirm which party pays.

faqs.q: Where did Medford get its name and what shaped its early housing?
faqs.a: Settlers renamed the Mistick settlement Meadford in the 1630s, and the name may refer to a meadow by a ford on the Mystic River. Farmland was divided into house lots from the 1840s and 1850s, so many Medford homes likely date from the 1800s and early 1900s. Older houses can carry repair needs that a cash buyer will price in.
The Mystic River flows from west to southeast through the middle of Medford. The Cradock Bridge carries Main Street over it into Medford Square, and a toll bridge stood on that site as early as 1637.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Medford house that I inherited?
faqs.a: Often yes, once whoever holds authority to sell has it, which may require probate. Speak with a Massachusetts attorney about that, then share the address and condition with us.
